name: John Miller's Tannery

documented_range.note: THE YEAR IS ATTESTED AND THE MONTH IS NOT, so the range opens on 1 January 1831 rather than claiming a build date. DRLOIH: 'In 1831 John Miller built a log house near his brother's tavern that he used as a tannery, Chicago's first recorded factory.' Andreas, independently and with a direction the other source lacks: 'John Miller, brother of Samuel, the landlord, came in 1831, and run a tannery just north of Miller's tavern.' THE END OF THE RANGE IS THE HONEST MINIMUM, NOT A FATE. Nothing reached follows this building past its founding: Andreas adds a partner, 'Benjamin Hall, tanner, a partner of John Miller, who came in 1832', and then the trade drops out of the record, while Samuel Miller — the brother whose tavern fixes this building's position — 'sold the tavern and moved away following the death of his wife in 1832'. So the anchor moved on three years before the scene date and the tannery's own survival rests on the ordinary continuity argument: a standing building stands until something says otherwise. Tagged inferred for that reason.

change_note: The log house John Miller built in 1831 just north of his brother's tavern and used as a tannery — the settlement's first recorded manufactory. The arrival of Benjamin Hall as his partner in 1832 is a change of business and does not open a new phase.

placement.position_note: PLACED 2026-08-11, AND IT IS A POSITION RELATIVE TO ANOTHER RECORD RATHER THAN TO ANY SURVIVING FEATURE. Andreas gives the direction — 'run a tannery just north of Miller's tavern' — and DRLOIH gives only proximity, 'near his brother's tavern'. Method: this project's own miller_house placement (local E +14, N +61, its north face on N +61) is taken as the anchor and this building is set 11.5 m north of that face on the same easting, so its south wall faces the tavern across a yard. THIS INHERITS EVERY UNCERTAINTY THE MILLER HOUSE CARRIES AND ADDS ONE. That record's own note says no surviving intersection locates it, that its coordinate comes from the datum origin and modern bank geometry, and that the along-bank axis is the softer one; on top of that, the 11.5 m separation recorded here is invented outright — 'just north' fixes a direction and no distance. Working uncertainty about 40 m, which is the Miller house's ~20 m plus the separation. WHY NORTH AND NOT INTO THE WATER: the point of land here is narrow, and the modelled 1834 waterline puts the North Branch about 40 m west of this building and the main stem about 15 m south of the tavern, so 'just north' is also the only direction with ground in it. A tannery is a nuisance trade — bark, lime and hides — and putting it behind the tavern rather than between the tavern and the water is consistent with that, but no source says so and it is not offered as evidence. Facade bearing 180, due south onto the tavern yard, inferred from nothing better than the building it is described against; nothing states which way it faced.
placement.symbolic_location: North bank at the forks, just north of Samuel Miller's house and tavern, on the point of land between the North Branch and the main stem.

footprint.note: PLACEHOLDER — NO DIMENSION IS ATTESTED and neither is the plan. What the sources give is a category: 'a log house ... that he used as a tannery'. 7 x 5.5 m is an ordinary single-pen log house of the type and period, chosen so that the building reads as a house put to a trade rather than as a purpose-built works, which is what the sources describe. Every number is invented. NOTE ALSO WHAT IS NOT DRAWN: a tannery is its yard — bark mill, lime pits, tan vats, drying sheds, and a water supply — and none of that is in this polygon or in the model. The record models the log house the sources name and nothing else. To resolve: any account of Miller and Hall's tanyard, or the Chicago Democrat's advertisements.

construction.note: 'built a log house near his brother's tavern that he used as a tannery' (DRLOIH). Andreas calls it a tannery and does not describe the fabric, so the log statement rests on the one source; it is consistent with everything else standing at the forks in 1831.

stories.note: Not attested. A single-pen log house is the near-universal form at the forks in 1831, and a building put to a trade is the last one anybody would raise a second storey on. Inference from the type, not from a statement about this building.

wall_height_m.note: No figure is attested. 2.5 m is about 8 ft: one storey of hewn-log wall plus a sill, the same reading and the same number this project gives Hogan's store and the Walker meeting house.

roof_type.note: Not attested. Gable is the near-universal roof form for log construction of this type, period and region.

roof_pitch_deg.note: No pitch is attested. 35 degrees is the archetype's mid-range for a low single-storey log building roofed in riven shakes. Inferred from construction practice, not measured.

chimneys.note: Not attested, and nothing describes a stack on this building. One is the normal number for a single-pen log house and the minimum for a building worked through Chicago winters. The COUNT is the inference; position, size and material are the archetype's — docs/LIBERTIES.md L26.

function.note: 'a log house ... that he used as a tannery, Chicago's first recorded factory' (DRLOIH); 'run a tannery just north of Miller's tavern' (Andreas). The function is the best-attested thing about this building and the model cannot show it: what stands is a log house, because a log house is what was built and because the yard that made it a tannery is not modelled. WHETHER IT WAS STILL TANNING ON 1835-07-01 IS UNATTESTED — Andreas's tanner partner arrives in 1832 and the trade then disappears from the record — so this value states what the building was for, not what it was doing on the scene date.

residents.name: The Miller and Hall tannery household
residents.why: 'A tannery just north of Miller's tavern' - the direction is the find that placed this dataset's record, and both men are named in it.

persons.name: John Miller
persons.note: ELECTED ONE OF THE FIVE FIRST TRUSTEES OF THE TOWN on 10 August 1833 with 20 of 28 votes, and Andreas notes that he 'being a candidate himself, refrained from voting' - so he is one of only two men in this parcel whose conduct at the poll is recorded. His brother Samuel Miller kept the tavern on the north bank at the forks and is not written as a household here, because Andreas's 1833 roster names him only in passing as 'Samuel, the landlord' and this project's miller_house record has the house 'past its innkeeping days' by the scene date. Andreas vol. 1, printed p. 132 (scan p. 281), 'an imperfect list of the denizens of the town in the fall of 1833, not before named' - a name, a trade and usually an arrival year, compiled fifty years after the fact. A YEAR off it is documented; a MONTH is not, and neither is anything about 1835. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 3 times: Poll list of the first election of the Board of Trustees of the Town of Chicago, 10 August 1833 — “Miller, John” (poll_1833_020, line 41); Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Miller, John” (tax_1833_074, line 126); Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Miller, John” (poll_1834_072, line 241). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Miller' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json). FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the city register of 1839 — “John Miller” as fire warden (f1839_r0033, printed page 38). What a match may carry, and it depends on WHICH TABLE it landed in. A match on printed page 38, or on any row of the mayors' table, is 1839-or-later evidence: it says the man held that office in that year and was therefore in Chicago in that year, it is written with the row's own describes_date and never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on it alone — a later appearance is corroboration of CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not of July 1835. A match on the sheriffs' rows of 1831, 1832, 1834 or 1836 is different in kind: the office is contemporary with the town, the 1834 row's term covers the scene date outright, and such a match carries reaches_scene. Even there the SOURCE is a retrospect — a table running to 1874, set in 1876 out of Old Settlers' recollections per the compiler's warning on printed page 3 — so it may be cited as a contemporary office and may not be graded `documented` without a second, nearer record. The ward on printed page 38 is a ward of the CITY of 1839 and places no house in the town of 1835. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Miller' folds to the same string as the register entry's, and the given name of both begins J. (data/research/directories/fergus_1839_election_crosswalk_1835.json and fergus_1839_register_crosswalk_1835.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

persons.name: Benjamin Hall
persons.note: A DOCUMENTED PARTNER IN THE SETTLEMENT'S FIRST MANUFACTORY. Andreas: 'The only manufactory established at that early day was the rude shed called a tannery, near the Miller tavern, where John Miller and Benjamin Hall were tanning a few hides into a rough but endurable leather.' He signed the 1832 militia agreement. FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the poll of Chicago's first city election, 2 May 1837 — “B. F. Hall” (f1839_v0626, printed page 45, ward 6, voting for William B. Ogden). What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago on 2 May 1837 and in that ward. It is written as 1837 evidence with describes_date 1837-05-02, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected_resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. The ward is a location in the CITY of 1837, whose six wards are drawn on printed page 46; it is not a location in the town of 1835 and does not place a house. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Hall' folds to the same string as the 1837 entry's, and the given name of both begins B. (data/research/directories/fergus_1839_election_crosswalk_1835.json and fergus_1839_register_crosswalk_1835.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

residents.research_note: THE SETTLEMENT'S FIRST FACTORY AND ITS TWO NAMED WORKMEN, in a household assembled from three passages - the roster, Bates's 1883 interview and Andreas's own summary of the settlement's industry. A TANNERY IS A POPULATION FACT AS WELL AS A BUILDING: it takes hides from the butchers (Archibald Clybourne has his own household here) and it supplies the saddlers at Lake and Canal (Goss & Cobb, also here), so three of this parcel's households are one supply chain. That is the sort of structure the inferred phase should be looking for when it decides which trades the town must have had.

"The Beginning of Wolf Point in Chicago, Illinois, including the history of the Wolf Point Tavern." Digital Research Library of Illinois History Journal.

research_note: THE SETTLEMENT'S FIRST FACTORY, AND A ONE-SENTENCE BUILDING: two sources, one sentence each, and between them a year, a builder, a fabric, a use and a direction. The direction is the find that placed it — Andreas's 'just north of Miller's tavern', which the project's dossier did not carry; docs/research/03-structures-north.md § 3.1 had only DRLOIH's 'near his brother's tavern'. Andreas also names the partner, Benjamin Hall, tanner, who came in 1832. EVERYTHING DIMENSIONAL IS INVENTED and the record says so attribute by attribute. The building is placed against another record rather than against the ground, so it moves if the Miller house moves. See docs/RESEARCH/miller_tannery.md.
